o: We need to scan the words of `text` and, whenever a word equals `first` and the immediately following word equals `second`, collect the word after that. In example 1, splitting gives `[alice, is, a, good, girl, she, is, a, good, student]`; at indices 2–3 we see `a good`, so index 4 (`girl`) is collected; at indices 7–8 we see `a good`, so index 9 (`student`) is collected. In example 2, `we will` appears at indices 0–1 and 3–4, yielding `we` and `rock`. Constraints are tiny (text length ≤ 1000), so any linear scan over words is more than sufficient.
k: Split the text into words once, then just compare adjacent triples by index.
Only iterate i up to len(words) - 3 to avoid out-of-bounds checks inside the loop.
String equality comparisons on short words make this an O(n) pass.

a.i: Splitting the text on spaces gives an array of words. A valid bigram at position i means words[i] == first and words[i+1] == second, in which case words[i+2] is a third to output. One linear scan with index bounds handled up front solves it.
s: Split text into a list of words.
For each index i from 0 to len(words) - 3:
If words[i] == first and words[i+1] == second, append words[i+2] to the answer.
a.t: O(n) where n is the length of text — splitting and one comparison pass over words.
a.sp: O(n) for the split word list and result array.

a.i: Instead of materializing all words, read tokens one at a time while remembering the previous two tokens. When prev2 == first and prev == second, the current token is a third. This uses constant extra memory beyond the answer and generalizes to streaming input.
s: Initialize prev2 and prev as empty strings.
Iterate over each token of the text (e.g., with a stringstream or manual tokenizer).
If prev2 == first and prev == second, append the current token to the result.
Shift prev2 = prev, prev = current token.
a.t: O(n) — single pass over the tokens of text.
a.sp: O(1) auxiliary space besides the output (Python/Java splits still cost O(n); C++ stringstream streams token by token).

w: In an interview, present Approach 1 first — it is the clearest and already optimal. Mention Approach 2 as a memory-conscious variant useful when the text arrives as a stream or cannot fit in memory. Pitfalls: iterating too far and indexing past the end of the word list (bound the loop at len - 3 / i + 2 < size); using == instead of .equals for Java strings; forgetting that overlapping matches like "a a a" with first="a", second="a" should yield ["a"] since windows shift by one. Edge cases: text shorter than three words returns an empty array; no matching bigram also returns empty. Follow-ups might ask for streaming input handling or case-insensitive matching.
